content: Amniotic fluid is a clear, watery liquid that surrounds and cushions a developing fetus within the amniotic sac, or amnion. This fluid allows the fetus to move freely without the uterine walls pressing tightly against its body, and it also provides buoyancy. The amnion begins to fill with fluid, primarily water, approximately two weeks after fertilization. By around 12 weeks of gestation, the amniotic fluid contains proteins, carbohydrates, lipids, phospholipids, urea, and electrolytes, all of which are essential for fetal growth and development. In the later stages of pregnancy, a significant portion of the amniotic fluid is composed of fetal urine. Recent research led by Anthony Atala from Wake Forest University and a team from Harvard University has identified amniotic fluid as a rich source of non-embryonic stem cells. These stem cells have demonstrated the ability to differentiate into various cell types, including brain, liver, and bone cells. When the amniotic sac ruptures, the forewaters are released, a phenomenon commonly referred to as a woman’s water breaking or spontaneous rupture of membranes (SROM). However, most of the hindwaters remain within the uterus until the baby is delivered. Complications Related to Amniotic Fluid Abnormal levels of amniotic fluid, whether too little (oligohydramnios) or too much (polyhydramnios or hydramnios), can indicate or cause complications for both the mother and the baby. While most pregnancies with these conditions proceed normally and result in the birth of a healthy baby, this is not always the case. Babies with insufficient amniotic fluid may develop limb contractures, clubbing of the hands and feet, or a life-threatening condition known as hypoplastic lungs. Hypoplastic lungs are underdeveloped and small, and this condition can be fatal, with affected babies often dying shortly after birth. During every prenatal visit, the obstetrician or gynecologist should measure the patient’s fundal height using a tape measure. Accurate measurement and documentation of fundal height are critical to ensure proper fetal growth and the progressive development of amniotic fluid. Routine ultrasounds should also be performed, as they provide additional information about fetal growth and amniotic fluid levels. Oligohydramnios can result from infections, kidney dysfunction or malformations (since fetal urine contributes significantly to amniotic fluid volume in later pregnancy), invasive procedures such as chorionic villus sampling (CVS), or preterm premature rupture of membranes (PPROM). Treatment for oligohydramnios may include bed rest, oral and intravenous hydration, antibiotics, steroids, or amnioinfusion. Polyhydramnios, on the other hand, is a risk factor for umbilical cord prolapse and is sometimes associated with macrosomic pregnancies (large babies). It is also linked to esophageal atresia, a congenital condition where the esophagus does not develop properly. Amniotic fluid is primarily produced by the mother until around 16 weeks of gestation. Preterm premature rupture of membranes (PPROM) occurs when the amniotic sac leaks fluid before 38 weeks of gestation. This condition can be caused by bacterial infections or structural defects in the amniotic sac, uterus, or cervix. In some cases, the leak may spontaneously heal, but in most instances of PPROM, labor begins within 48 hours of membrane rupture. When this occurs, it is essential to provide the mother with treatment to prevent potential infections in the newborn. A rare but often fatal obstetric complication is an amniotic fluid embolism, which can lead to disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), a severe and life-threatening condition.
